passages.label: A
passages.text: A participant in swimming follows a line in the water. An Olympic climber studies a wall. At Paris 2024, people could compete in Boulder and Lead or race in Speed. These are modern Olympic events. The ancient Games had very different activities, and even at the same modern competition each climbing event has a different task.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A Boulder and Lead event has two parts, a semifinal and a final. Points from both stages give one ranking in each part. The best final score wins. All finalists start again at zero.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Boulder climbing takes place on a low wall. Mats below it help protect people if they fall. Each course presents four problems. A challenging move may take more than one attempt. The aim is to control the highest scoring hold, a place to grip the wall.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Lead climbing uses a taller wall and a longer route. They try to climb as high as possible before they fall or stop. In the semifinal, they start in the reverse order of Olympic seeding. This is a ranking made before the event. In the last part, the order follows that result. Each person tries the route alone and cannot watch another person first. A person needs to be fit enough to move quickly and retain control. In a hard move, a climber may appear to throw their weight toward a hold, and a rope or mat helps limit the effect of an accident.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A fan watching from below can see why an intelligent choice matters as much as a strong arm. In Lead, climbers score by reaching holds on the wall. A hand can hit a hold without taking control of it. The person who eventually becomes champion uses both strength and careful movement.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Speed was a separate event at Paris 2024. In heats and finals, two people raced on the same standard wall. Each used a different lane. Their aim was simple. They wanted to reach the top first.

passages.label: G
passages.text: The three kinds need different skills. Boulder climbers make careful choices on short problems. Lead climbers keep going on a long route. Speed climbers move quickly on a fixed wall. The sport can seem strange to a new viewer. Every event has a goal, a set place, and rules.

passages.label: H
passages.text: A person learning the sport can take a lesson even if a local gym may charge for it. The cost of practice is separate from a medal or prize. An athlete may also have a salary from other work. Someone who learns to kick in swimming may need to learn a different way to move both feet for a climb. Coaches and families can support that training.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Open-water swimming can look strange to someone who usually watches a pool race, and a participant can follow a line in a pool or climb out by a ladder. Even if a competition takes place near an ancient town, the people in the water have to follow its marks. Once swimmers compete, those points show them which way to go.

passages.label: B
passages.text: World Aquatics says participants must complete the whole course in freestyle. Turning buoys are floating markers that tell a swimmer where to turn. Miss a turn and a fast person can lose time.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Swimmers kick to stay moving. It helps to be strong when lifting the head to look. A swimmer could hit a buoy by going too close. A fan may expect the fastest person to win. An intelligent choice of route may help a future champion swim less far. The shortest route can be hard to see.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Before a race, organisers evaluate the water and course. In Singapore in 2025, the organisation postponed the 10km event when water tests did not meet the required standards. Later tests improved. The races went ahead that afternoon, and this shows why plans may change before an event in natural water, and a marked course can still be challenging. Safety teams watch the race. If someone has an accident, a helper can throw a float to that person, and the marks give other people room to go on.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Races have different lengths. Singapore 2025 included a 5km race and a mixed relay. A swimmer must be fit, but judging the course and the position of others can matter as much as a strong finish.

passages.label: F
passages.text: World Aquatics updated its open-water rules for 2025. The update included the 3km Individual Knockout Sprint. It also added a Video Review Judge, an official who uses video to help check results. Officials use more than a finish line to manage a race. Clear decisions help people compete fairly when many reach a turn together.

passages.label: G
passages.text: A manual from World Aquatics in 2020 describes support around the route. Safety boats and trained staff need clear roles and communication. Rescue boats should carry a driver and a lifeguard. They give help if an accident happens or a person is in trouble. Planning includes knowing how to bring someone back to shore.

passages.label: H
passages.text: Some organisers charge to enter. The cost depends on the race. The money can support safety staff. A race may offer a prize. Many swimmers only want to reach the finish. A regular salary is something a person earns through work. A team may score points in several races. The records also show which swimmer came in first.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A Spartan Race is an obstacle course race. The group offers several race types, so a detail about one type does not describe every race. The Sprint is sold as a 5K race with 20 obstacles, a separate event from the longer races. The Sprint has trail running and obstacles on off-road ground. The ground can include water and mud. Runners move across natural ground and complete separate tasks. The event can feel challenging because running is only one part.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A person on a Sprint may have to climb over a wall or carry an object. Someone with a strong grip may know when to use both hands. An intelligent choice of where to put a foot could matter more than using force. A runner who can kick a ball or hit a tennis ball in another sport may find that the same skills only help with part of this race.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Spear Throw is another well-known obstacle. The athlete chooses a spear and throws it at a target 25 feet away. The spear must stick in the target without falling out. This may seem strange to a runner who expects only a trail race. It changes the rhythm of the course. The person must slow down, aim, and then continue. A throw only succeeds if the spear stays in the target.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Every obstacle can produce a penalty if a person fails to complete it. And the arrangements vary across categories. Some racers run a penalty loop, whereas a Stadion race can require fifteen burpees. In practice a person can score points by finishing a series of obstacles, while a fan may watch a champion to understand how decisions change with each challenge. Friends can support a runner by encouraging them where the rules allow it. Organisers may charge an entry fee, adding to the cost of equipment and transport. A prize and a regular salary are separate amounts to consider when planning how often to compete.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A participant who is fit for swimming or distance running may still find a wall or spear hard to manage. Each race can take place in a different setting. And the course has instructions that help keep the tasks in order. The name Spartan can recall ancient Sparta. The present competition is a modern event with its own rules. Sensible preparation matters because a tired runner who rushes an obstacle may have an accident. Training across more than one activity gives people who compete more ways to move with care.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What should a runner conclude about other Spartan events from the Sprint description?
options: A longer event must also have exactly twenty obstacles.
The 5K and twenty tasks describe the Sprint, while a different type can have other details.
The Sprint is described as the only type of race held on outdoor ground.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can trail running on this course require more than moving quickly on uneven ground?
options: The passage says runners stay on a flat track between every task.
Some parts are timed only by how quickly the entrant can throw an object.
There are separate challenges to complete in addition to running over the ground.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What example does the text give of a choice that can matter more than force?
options: Deciding where to place a foot.
Treating every obstacle as if it required maximum strength.
Copying the motion used to score in a different sport without adapting it.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A participant has learnt one sort of movement very well elsewhere. What might limit how much advantage that gives here?
options: A person who plays another game is barred from trying a course like this.
Skills become irrelevant the moment the runner reaches natural ground.
The new tasks involve a variety of movements, and the ability brought to the course may fit only part of that mix.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a completed attempt from a mere hit in the throwing example?
options: A hit counts even if the object falls straight out.
The object has to remain where it landed in the target.
The result depends only on how fast the runner arrives at the task.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What example shows why a penalty cannot be assumed to be the same for all events?
options: Some people run an extra loop, and another type can require a set of exercises.
Every course uses the same loop even when a different consequence is stated.
The only consequence in any event is paying the original entry fee.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What expense does the article give in addition to equipment and transport?
options: A salary that is paid to every competitor.
A payment that makes the rules optional for a team.
A fee for entering the event.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the reference to ancient Sparta establish about the present race?
options: The name can recall Sparta even though the actual event follows modern rules of its own.
The race treats any action once practised in Sparta as part of the rules today.
The date the event was designed is fixed by the age of the name.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A runner is tiring, and the next task calls for a way of moving they have not used on the course. What would have been useful to do in advance?
options: Train the strongest movement alone and try to go faster at every task.
Work on a variety of movements and practise using them without rushing.
Assume the action required by a new obstacle will be identical to the previous one.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the guidance for thinking about the whole event?
options: Understanding one race type establishes that every other course has the same tasks and penalties.
Preparing for the straight running section is enough for every other part of the event.
Check the kind of race and its requirements, then prepare for a range of tasks as well as the running.
